```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")
library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("bolivian_highlands.json5")
set_data <- read_json_file("bolivian_highlands_settlements.json")
led_data <- read_json_file("bolivian_highlands_source_ledger.json5")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("%", "\\\\%", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("#", "\\\\#", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
all_years <- names(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark)
tot_1500 <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1500"]])
tot_1535 <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1535"]])
tot_800 <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["800"]])
tot_area <- as.numeric(mod_data$total_area_km2)
```

# Abstract

The Bolivian Highlands (405,4k km², encompassing 405.375 km² and 5.001 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) constitute the southern demographic pivot of the Central Andes. Stretching from the lacustrine raised-field plains of Lake Titicaca across the high-altitude pastoral plateau of Oruro and Lake Poopó into the fertile maize-producing inter-Andean valleys of La Paz, Cochabamba, Chuquisaca, Potosí and Tarija, this highland theatre sustained one of the densest pre-Columbian agrarian populations in South America. For more than three millennia before the Spanish arrival in 1535AD, highland societies harnessed frost-resistant tuber agriculture, quinoa cultivation, freeze-dried food preservation, camelid herding and vertical ecological complementarity to overcome altitudes between 2.500 m and 4.300 m, creating demographic densities far exceeding those of the adjacent tropical lowlands of Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz.

Reconstructed across twenty-two benchmark horizons from 10000BC to 1535AD under PRETA, the aggregate population of the Bolivian Highlands expanded from 7,05k early Holocene hunter-gatherers in 10000BC to 57,4k in 5000BC and 193,1k in 2000BC as camelid domestication and sedentary lake-shore villages took hold across Chiripa, the Taraco Peninsula and the Wankarani mounds of Oruro. Formative nucleation raised regional totals to 304,2k in 1000BC and 528,8k by 0AD. During the Middle Horizon, the expansion of the Tiwanaku state from its Lake Titicaca hearth across Cochabamba, the Yungas and southern intermontane corridors lifted highland population to 1,03M in 600AD and 1,20M at the imperial apogee of 800AD to 1000AD. Following the eleventh-century fragmentation of Tiwanaku and prolonged Altiplano drought, settlement decentralised into fortified hilltop capitals (*pukaras*) and Aymara confederations — Pacajes, Omasuyos, Carangas, Sora, Quillacas, Qaraqara, Charka, Yampara and Chichas — maintaining 1,24M inhabitants by 1200AD before Inca *Tawantinsuyu* integration under *Qullasuyu* lifted the highland total to a pre-contact peak of 1,41M inhabitants in 1500AD (347,83 persons per 100 km² across the entire highland domain, and over 1.200 persons per 100 km² in the Lake Titicaca littoral). Following the Andean smallpox epidemic of the 1520s and the Spanish entry into Charcas, population stood at 1,25M in 1535AD.

This chapter establishes the first comprehensive regional demographic synthesis and 316-settlement gazetteer for the Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands within PRETA, reconciling 646 audited candidates from the Bolivian Radiocarbon Database, XRONOS chronometric records, regional Titicaca and Altiplano settlement surveys, OpenStreetMap and Wikidata monument inventories and published Bolivian archaeological monographs. Partitioned organically across six HydroBASINS Level 6 watershed divisions, the reconstruction directly resolves prior highland-to-lowland density inversions across Bolivia while preserving the distinct urban savanna achievements of lowland Llanos de Moxos in the neighbouring Western Amazon Basin chapter.

# High-Altitude Ecology and Vertical Complementarity

## The Altiplano and Inter-Andean Valley Gradient

Unlike temperate mid-latitude mountains where biological productivity collapses sharply above 2.500 m, the Tropical Andes of Bolivia exhibit an extraordinarily broad altitudinal habitability belt extending from 1.800 m up to 4.300 m [@Kolata1993; @Capriles2023Review]. Two physical mechanisms explain this demographic paradox. First, tropical solar insolation ensures reliable daytime warmth throughout the year even on the high plateau, allowing cold-adapted domesticates — hundreds of landraces of potato (*Solanum tuberosum*), oca, ulluco, quinoa (*Chenopodium quinoa*) and cañiwa — to mature reliably up to 4.100 m [@Janusek2008; @Bandy2001]. Second, Lake Titicaca (8.372 km² at 3.812 m elevation) acts as an enormous thermal reservoir that buffers nocturnal frost across its littoral plains, lengthening the frost-free growing season by more than forty days relative to the southern Altiplano [@Kolata1993; @Guedron2023].

To the east of the Cordillera Real and Cordillera Central, steep tectonic canyons plunge from 4.500 m glacier-fed peaks into temperate *quechua* and *valle* basins between 2.000 m and 3.000 m (Cochabamba, Mizque, Chuquisaca, Cinti and Tarija) and warm *yungas* cloud-forest terraces between 1.200 m and 2.200 m (Coroico, Chulumani, Larecaja and Apolobamba). Rather than existing as isolated ecological niches, these altitudinal tiers were knitted together by what John Murra defined as the vertical archipelago: highland Altiplano polities systematically stationed permanent colonies (*mitmaqkuna*) in eastern maize and coca valleys while valley communities exchanged grain, wood, chilli peppers and coca leaf for highland freeze-dried potatoes (*chuño*), camelid jerky (*charqui*), salt from Uyuni and Coipasa, obsidian and copper-tin bronze [@Murra1972; @PlattBouysseHarris2006]. This vertical integration multiplied the effective carrying capacity of every highland watershed far beyond what local rainfall or elevation alone would imply.

## Six Organic Hydrological Divisions

In accordance with PRETA's hydrological partitioning framework for pre-colonial landscapes, the Bolivian Highlands are divided into six organic HydroBASINS Level 6 watershed units cleanly separated from the lowland Amazonian savannas of Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Lake Titicaca Basin and Tiwanaku Core

Covering the Bolivian endorheic drainage of Lake Titicaca, the Taraco Peninsula, the Katari Basin, the Tiwanaku Valley, the Copacabana Peninsula and the upper Desaguadero outlet (32.456 km²), this compact lacustrine hearth sustained the highest sustained population density anywhere in pre-Columbian Bolivia [@Kolata1993; @Stanish2003; @AlbarracinJordan1992]. Early Formative farming villages at Chiripa and Kala Uyuni expanded rapidly during the first millennium BC [@Bandy2001; @Bandy2004], giving rise to the monumental urban capital of Tiwanaku (reaching 35,0k inhabitants by 800AD) and its secondary lacustrine centre at Lukurmata (11,0k) [@Bermann1994; @Janusek2004]. Supported by more than 19.000 hectares of heat-retaining raised agricultural fields (*suka kollus*) across the Koani and Tiwanaku plains, the division peaked near 307k inhabitants during the Tiwanaku Middle Horizon apogee (800AD to 1000AD) and reached 320k by 1500AD under Inca *Qullasuyu* administration (985,95 persons per 100 km²).

### Chuquiabo (La Paz), Larecaja (Iskanwaya) and Yungas Valleys

Encompassing the headwater canyons of the Río La Paz, Boopi, Mapiri and Consata draining off the eastern flanks of Mount Illampu and Mount Illimani (50.659 km²), this division combined high-altitude pastoralism along the Cordillera Real with intensive terraced maize and coca cultivation in the Yungas and Larecaja valleys. Archaeological surveys document major Late Intermediate Mollo stone citadels at Iskanwaya (5,2k peak) and Aucapata alongside ancestral Kallawaya terraced valleys around Charazani and Curva, while the sheltered Choqueyapu basin of Chuquiabo (La Paz, 14,5k peak) anchored gold-washing, caravan exchange and royal coca estates along the pre-Hispanic Takesi stone highway to Chulumani and Coroico [@Parssinen2005; @Capriles2023Review]. Population expanded steadily from 87,5k in 0AD to 205k in 1000AD and 250k in 1500AD (493,50 persons per 100 km²).

### Central Altiplano: Wankarani, Paria (Oruro), Poopó and Carangas

Spanning the central endorheic plateau around Lake Poopó, the middle Desaguadero River and the volcanic western sierra of Carangas (62.662 km²), this division was the cradle of the Formative Wankarani tradition (1500BC to 200AD), characterised by scores of stratified adobe-mound villages at La Joya, Iroco and Caracollo combining camelid pastoralism, llama-caravan exchange and early copper smelting [@McAndrews2005; @Capriles2014Wankarani]. During the Late Intermediate Period, powerful Aymara señoríos — Sora, Carangas and Quillacas — built extensive polychrome *chullpa* burial towers across Curahuara de Carangas, Corque and Turco and fortified stone towns such as Alcaya above the inter-salar quinoa plains. Under Inca rule, Paria (9,8k peak) became the premier *Qullasuyu* provincial capital and *Qhapaq Ñan* storage hub [@GyarmatiCondarco2014]. Regional totals reached 177,6k in 800AD and 185k by 1500AD (295,23 persons per 100 km²).

### Cochabamba, Incallajta and Mizque Inter-Andean Valleys

Draining the fertile headwater valleys of the Río Rocha, Cliza, Arque and Mizque into the upper Río Grande (78.477 km²), Cochabamba constituted the agricultural breadbasket of the Bolivian Andes [@GyarmatiVarga1999]. Beginning around 500AD, Tiwanaku state colonists established intensive maize enclaves throughout the Central Valley (Sierra Mokho) and Valle Alto (Cliza, Punata, Tarata and Mizque), generating a distinctive Tiwanaku-derived polychrome ceramic tradition. In the late fifteenth century, the Inca emperor Huayna Capac transformed the Cochabamba basin into a vast state estate worked by fourteen thousand *mitmaqkuna* colonists drawn from across the Altiplano, supported by more than 2.400 circular *qollqa* grain storehouses at Cotapachi near Quillacollo and guarded along the eastern cloud-forest rim by the monumental fortress-city of Incallajta (8,8k) and the carved sanctuary of El Fuerte de Samaipata [@GyarmatiVarga1999; @Cobos2004]. Population reached 233k in 800AD and 295k in 1500AD (375,91 persons per 100 km²).

### Charcas, Qaraqara, Yampara, Chuquisaca, Porco and Potosí Sierra

Extending across the dissected highland plateaus and upper Pilcomayo valleys of Northern Potosí and Chuquisaca (71.564 km²), this division was the heartland of the warrior-mining confederations of the Charka (centred on Sacaca and Chayanta), Qaraqara (centred on Macha, Pocoata and Porco) and Yampara (centred on Choquechaca-Chuquisaca, Tarabuco and Yamparáez) [@PlattBouysseHarris2006; @Alconini2016]. Before Spanish conquest, the Qaraqara worked rich silver veins at Porco (6,8k peak) for the Inca state using wind-blown *huayra* smelting furnaces [@VanBuren2003], while the Incas built the massive plateau fortress of Oroncota (5,8k) overlooking the Pilcomayo canyon to shield Charcas against Chiriguano incursions from the Chaco [@Alconini2004]. Surveys by Lecoq and Céspedes in Yura and southern Potosí confirm dense hilltop *pukara* and terraced agricultural networks extending into Cotagaita and Tupiza [@LecoqCespedes1997]. Regional totals reached 197,5k in 800AD and 250k in 1500AD (349,34 persons per 100 km²).

### Southern Altiplano (Uyuni and Lípez), Cinti and Tarija Valleys

Covering the arid southern salar plateau of Uyuni and Lípez alongside the deeply incised irrigated canyons of Cinti (Camargo, San Lucas) and the temperate Guadalquivir valley of Tarija (109.557 km²), this southern division linked the Bolivian Altiplano to northwestern Argentina and the Atacama littoral [@Nielsen2002]. Despite extreme aridity across the high Lípez puna (4.000 m to 4.500 m), agro-pastoral caravan towns at San Cristóbal de Lípez, San Pablo de Lípez, Colcha K and Llica prospered on salt, copper and obsidian transport [@Nielsen2002], while lower irrigated valleys at Tarija-Tolomosa (5,8k), San Lorenzo and Camargo sustained dense Chichas and Tomata maize-farming communities. Aggregate population reached 86,9k in 800AD and 110k in 1500AD (100,40 persons per 100 km²).

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  p_0 <- as.numeric(r$population[["0"]])
  p_800 <- as.numeric(r$population[["800"]])
  p_1500 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1500"]])
  a_km2 <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  d_1500 <- (p_1500 / a_km2) * 100
  data.frame(
    Division = clean_text(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(a_km2, 0L),
    Pop0AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_0),
    Pop800AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_800),
    Pop1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1500),
    Dens1500 = viscount_fmt_number(d_1500, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, rows)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, data.frame(
  Division = "Total Bolivian Highlands",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L),
  Pop0AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["0"]])),
  Pop800AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_800),
  Pop1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1500),
  Dens1500 = viscount_fmt_number((tot_1500 / tot_area) * 100, 1L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands hydrological divisions, land areas (km²), benchmark populations (0AD, 800AD Tiwanaku peak, 1500AD Inca Qullasuyu peak) and 1500AD population density (inhabitants per 100 km²).",
  c("Hydrological Division", "Area (km²)", "0AD", "800AD", "1500AD", "Dens. 1500"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize", scale_to_fit = TRUE)
)
```

# Chronological Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 1535AD)

## Archaic Foragers and Early Camelid Domestication (10000BC to 2000BC)

Radiocarbon records assembled in the Bolivian Radiocarbon Database confirm human occupation across the Altiplano and southern rock-shelters by the terminal Pleistocene [@Capriles2023BRD; @Capriles2023Review]. Early Holocene bands hunted vicuña, guanaco and taruca deer along high-altitude bofedal wetlands and shrinking Pleistocene palaeolakes (Tauca and Coipasa), maintaining small mobile populations estimated at 7,05k across the Bolivian Highlands in 10000BC and 16,9k by 8000BC. During the Middle Holocene arid phase (6000BC to 3500BC), shrinking interior lakes drew hunter-pastoralists toward the permanent littoral of Lake Titicaca, springs in the Central Altiplano and sheltered intermontane valleys [@Guedron2023]. By 3000BC, selective management of domesticated llamas and alpacas alongside early chenopod and tuber cultivation lifted the highland population to 128,4k, reaching 193,1k by 2000BC.

## Formative Sedentism: Chiripa, Taraco and Wankarani (2000BC to 300AD)

Between 1500BC and 200AD, two parallel Formative trajectories transformed highland demography. Around the southern shores of Lake Titicaca, pedestrian surveys by Bandy on the Taraco Peninsula and Albarracín-Jordán in the Lower Tiwanaku Valley reveal rapid village multiplication and regular fissioning once settlements exceeded roughly 200 to 300 inhabitants [@Bandy2001; @Bandy2004; @AlbarracinJordan1992]. Civic-ceremonial sunken courts at Chiripa, Kala Uyuni and Khonkho Wankane anchored growing agrarian chiefdoms whose surplus supported craft specialisation and obsidian exchange [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2004]. Simultaneously on the central plateau of Oruro, Wankarani agro-pastoral communities established dozens of permanent circular-house mound settlements near bofedal pastures [@McAndrews2005; @Capriles2014Wankarani]. Aggregate population rose from 304,2k in 1000BC to 528,8k at 0AD and 656,1k by 200AD.

## The Tiwanaku State and Middle Horizon Apogee (300AD to 1050AD)

From roughly 400AD onward, Tiwanaku consolidated political and ritual supremacy across the southern Titicaca Basin, growing into a planned ceremonial metropolis covering more than four square kilometres and housing approximately 35,0k urban residents flanked by a dense rural hinterland of satellite towns such as Lukurmata (11,0k) and Pajchiri (3,4k) [@Kolata1993; @Janusek2004; @Marsh2023Tiwanaku]. Monumental sunken-court complexes — Kalasasaya, Akapana, Puma Punku and Putuni — coexisted with vast engineered expanses of raised agricultural fields (*suka kollus*) whose water canals buffered crops against nocturnal freezing and multiplied potato and quinoa yields [@Kolata1993]. Tiwanaku demographic influence extended far beyond the Altiplano through direct agrarian colonies in Cochabamba, Mizque and the Yungas, lifting overall Bolivian Highland population from 821,7k in 400AD to 1,03M in 600AD and 1,20M across the 800AD to 1000AD imperial peak.

## Late Intermediate Aymara Señoríos and Hillfort Nucleation (1050AD to 1450AD)

Bayesian radiocarbon analyses and lake-core palaeoclimate reconstructions indicate that severe multi-decadal drought around 1050AD to 1150AD disrupted raised-field hydraulics across the southern Titicaca plains, precipitating the political dissolution of the Tiwanaku state [@Guedron2023; @Marsh2023Tiwanaku]. Crucially, however, regional surveys demonstrate that political collapse did not produce demographic emptiness [@Stanish2003; @Arkush2011]. Rather, population redistributed from exposed lacustrine plains onto defensible hilltop *pukaras*, terraced eastern valleys and pastoral upland settlements organised into competing Aymara and Uru-Puquina confederations — Pacajes, Omasuyos, Carangas, Sora, Quillacas, Charka, Qaraqara, Yampara and Chichas [@Parssinen2005; @PlattBouysseHarris2006; @Arkush2011]. After a modest eleventh-century trough around 1,19M in 1100AD, territorial resilience and expanded valley maize cultivation drove renewed expansion to 1,24M in 1200AD, 1,30M in 1300AD and 1,36M in 1400AD.

## Inca Qullasuyu and the Eve of Spanish Conquest (1450AD to 1535AD)

Incorporation into the southern quarter (*Qullasuyu*) of *Tawantinsuyu* during the mid-fifteenth century integrated the Bolivian Highlands into an unprecedented imperial logistics network. Along the twin branches of the *Qhapaq Ñan* hugging both flanks of Lake Titicaca and descending through Paria, Macha, Porco and Cotagaita, the Incas founded administrative capitals, state pilgrimage shrines on the Islands of the Sun and Moon, thousands of maize *qollqas* in Cochabamba and defensive eastern border fortresses at Incallajta, Samaipata and Oroncota [@BauerStanish2001; @GyarmatiVarga1999; @GyarmatiCondarco2014; @Alconini2004]. Highland population reached its pre-Columbian zenith of 1,41M inhabitants in 1500AD (Figure \ref{fig:traj}). Even before Diego de Almagro's expedition marched down the Altiplano in 1535AD, Old World smallpox introduced along Andean trade routes in the mid-1520s — compounded by the brutal Huascar-Atahualpa civil war — reduced highland totals by roughly 11% to 1,25M inhabitants on the threshold of colonial rule.

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
show_yrs <- c("-10000", "-5000", "-2000", "-1000", "0", "400", "800", "1000", "1200", "1400", "1500", "1535")
b_rows <- lapply(show_yrs, function (yk) {
  tot <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  lo <- sum(vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$population_bounds[[yk]][[1]]), numeric(1)))
  hi <- sum(vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$population_bounds[[yk]][[2]]), numeric(1)))
  dens <- (tot / tot_area) * 100
  data.frame(
    Year = fmt_yr(yk),
    Total = viscount_fmt_pop(tot),
    Low = viscount_fmt_pop(lo),
    High = viscount_fmt_pop(hi),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, b_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Long-run pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands demographic benchmarks (10000BC to 1535AD) with asymmetric empirical uncertainty bounds and density per 100 km².",
  c("Benchmark", "Headline Pop.", "Lower Bound", "Upper Bound", "Dens. / 100 km²"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Highlands versus Lowlands in Pre-Columbian Bolivia

Reconciling the Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands (1,41M inhabitants across 405,4k km² in 1500AD, averaging 347,83 persons per 100 km²) against the Bolivian tropical lowlands included in PRETA's Western Amazon Basin chapter (Llanos de Moxos, Beni, Pando and eastern Santa Cruz, peaking around 345k to 380k across more than 700k km² of seasonal savannas and forest) resolves a persistent cartographic distortion in South American spatial demography. While Casarabe monumental mounds and raised fields in Llanos de Moxos represent a remarkable pre-Columbian lowland urban civilisation, absolute and relative population densities remained overwhelmingly concentrated in the Andean highlands and inter-Andean valleys. Across Bolivia as a whole in 1500AD, roughly 80% of all inhabitants resided in the Altiplano and Cordillera divisions, where mean areal density stood nearly ten times higher than in the eastern lowlands and more than twenty times higher in the Lake Titicaca littoral.

This empirical hierarchy also mirrors the early colonial fiscal geography documented immediately after 1535AD. When Viceroy Francisco de Toledo conducted the *Visita General* of 1572AD to 1575AD across Upper Peru, the highland provinces of La Paz, Omasuyos, Pacajes, Paria, Carangas, Cochabamba, Chayanta, Charcas and Chichas yielded hundreds of thousands of enumerated tributaries and supplied the vast rotational labour force of the Potosí silver mines, whereas the eastern lowlands remained a sparse missionary frontier until the late seventeenth century [@PlattBouysseHarris2006; @Capriles2023Review]. By assembling a dedicated Bolivian Highlands gazetteer, integrating the Bolivian Radiocarbon Database and XRONOS records and isolating highland watersheds from lowland earthwork belts, PRETA restores full historical fidelity across the entire Bolivian Andes-to-Amazon transect.

# Archaeological Sources and Spatial Conditioning

## Institutional Registries and Radiocarbon Taphonomy

Any demographic reconstruction of the Bolivian Highlands confronts an acute institutional asymmetry compared with neighbouring Andean republics. Whereas Peru's Ministry of Culture maintains an openly queryable national GIS portal exceeding twenty-eight thousand pre-Hispanic monument records and Colombia's ICANH publishes over twenty-two thousand georeferenced archaeological sites, Bolivia's national archaeological inventory (SIAAB) remains legally restricted under Law 530 of 2014 to deter clandestine looting. Relying uncritically on international heritage portals without correcting for this regulatory gap artificially depresses Highland Bolivia by an order of magnitude relative to adjacent Peruvian catchments across Lake Titicaca and even below heavily remote-sensed lowland earthwork belts in Beni and Acre.

To overcome this bias rigorously without resorting to synthetic extrapolation, PRETA triangulates five independent empirical evidence streams [@Capriles2023BRD; @Capriles2023Review; @Stanish2003]:

1. **Countrywide Radiocarbon Synthesis**: The Bolivian Radiocarbon Database compiled by Capriles and indexed through XRONOS provides hundreds of vetted chronometric determinations spanning early Holocene Altiplano rock-shelters, Formative Wankarani and Chiripa villages, Middle Horizon Tiwanaku monumental strata and Late Intermediate valley settlements [@Capriles2023BRD; @Marsh2019Tiwanaku].
2. **Full-Coverage Regional Pedestrian Surveys**: Intensive walking surveys covering the Taraco Peninsula [@Bandy2001], the Lower and Middle Tiwanaku Valley [@AlbarracinJordan1992], the Katari Basin around Lukurmata [@Bermann1994; @Janusek2004], the Island of the Sun [@BauerStanish2001], Pacajes-Caquiaviri [@Parssinen2005], the Wankarani plateau of La Joya and Iroco [@McAndrews2005; @Capriles2014Wankarani], Paria [@GyarmatiCondarco2014], Cochabamba [@GyarmatiVarga1999], Yampara-Oroncota [@Alconini2004; @Alconini2016], Yura-Potosí [@LecoqCespedes1997] and Lípez [@Nielsen2002] supply direct site-area measurements and phase-by-phase settlement counts.
3. **Satellite and Monument Inventories**: Georeferenced OpenStreetMap and Wikidata archaeological monuments (419 records across Bolivia and the Titicaca littoral) corroborate hilltop *pukara* fortifications, *chullpa* necropolises, agricultural terrace networks and *Qhapaq Ñan* road segments [@Arkush2011].
4. **Ethnohistorical *Marka* Continuity**: Early colonial *visitas* and tributary registers from 1548AD to 1575AD confirm the unbroken geographic continuity of major Aymara and Quechua *cabeceras* — including Achacachi, Caquiaviri, Viacha, Sica Sica, Paria, Challapata, Curahuara de Carangas, Macha, Sacaca, Chayanta, Tarabuco, Porco, Cotagaita and Tupiza — directly linking pre-Hispanic settlement hubs to their colonial successors [@PlattBouysseHarris2006; @Parssinen2005].
5. **Sliver-Merged Hydrological Conditioning**: Within PRETA's non-stationary Matérn kriging pipeline, HydroBASINS Level 6 confluence slivers smaller than 2.200 km² are folded into adjacent same-biome catchments and taphonomic shrinkage is applied to areal site density rather than raw counts, ensuring that small lowland river junctions never manufacture spurious density peaks above Tiwanaku, La Paz, Cochabamba or Chuquisaca.

## Agro-Pastoral Carrying Capacity and Urban Rank-Size Structure

Settlement sizes across the Bolivian Highlands followed a pronounced primate-to-polycentric rank-size evolution closely tied to imperial integration. During the Early and Middle Formative (1500BC to 200AD), Lake Titicaca villages rarely exceeded 500 to 1.500 inhabitants before scalar stress triggered community fissioning [@Bandy2004]. Between 500AD and 950AD, Tiwanaku shattered this ceiling, concentrating an estimated 30k to 40k residents inside a gridded urban core surrounded by moat-bounded ceremonial precincts, residential *barrios* of craft specialists and satellite lacustrine towns such as Lukurmata (11,0k) and Pajchiri (3,4k) [@Kolata1993; @Janusek2004; @Marsh2023Tiwanaku]. Experimental reconstructions of Lake Titicaca raised-field agriculture indicate sustained potato yields between 10 and 20 metric tonnes per hectare — three to four times dryland Altiplano productivity — easily capable of feeding well over 250k inhabitants across the Bolivian Titicaca littoral alone [@Kolata1993].

Following eleventh-century aridification and Tiwanaku's political dissolution, urban primacy flattened into a polycentric network of fortified regional centres across the Aymara señoríos [@Arkush2011; @Guedron2023]. Under fifteenth-century Inca *Qullasuyu*, imperial administration re-established a tiered urban hierarchy linking terraced valley granaries in Cochabamba (Sierra Mokho 18,5k, Quillacollo-Cotapachi 12,0k, Sacaba 6,8k, Punata 6,4k, Cliza 6,2k) with Altiplano *Qhapaq Ñan* administrative capitals (Chuquiabo-La Paz 14,5k, Paria 9,8k, Copacabana 7,5k, Achacachi 5,6k, Caquiaviri 5,2k), eastern frontier citadels (Incallajta 8,8k, Oroncota 5,8k, Samaipata 5,6k, Iskanwaya 5,2k) and metallurgical hubs in Charcas (Choquechaca-Chuquisaca 11,5k, Porco 6,8k, Sacaca 5,8k, Macha 5,6k).

```{r tbl-top-sites, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
pks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(pks, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(18L, length(set_list)))]
reg_lbls <- list(
  bolhi_titicaca_tiwanaku = "Titicaca & Tiwanaku",
  bolhi_la_paz_yungas_larecaja = "La Paz & Yungas",
  bolhi_oruro_poopo_carangas = "Oruro & Carangas",
  bolhi_cochabamba_mizque_valleys = "Cochabamba & Mizque",
  bolhi_charcas_potosi_chuquisaca = "Charcas & Potosí",
  bolhi_southern_altiplano_tarija = "Lípez & Tarija"
)
top_rows <- lapply(ord, function (i) {
  s <- set_list[[i]]
  yrs <- sort(as.numeric(names(s$population)))
  rk <- if (!is.null(s$region_id)) s$region_id else s$region
  data.frame(
    Settlement = clean_text(s$name),
    Division = if (!is.null(reg_lbls[[rk]])) reg_lbls[[rk]] else clean_text(rk),
    Span = paste0(fmt_yr(min(yrs)), "--", fmt_yr(max(yrs))),
    Peak = viscount_fmt_pop(max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading eighteen pre-Columbian settlements of the Bolivian Highlands ranked by peak population (10000BC to 1535AD).",
  c("Settlement", "Hydrological Division", "Attested Span", "Peak Pop."),
  list(label = "tab:top-sites", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Vertical Complementarity, Caravan Networks and Metallurgical Landscapes

Long-term demographic resilience across the Bolivian Highlands depended on institutionalised vertical complementarity (*control vertical de un máximo de pisos ecológicos*) uniting high-altitude *puna* herding with temperate inter-Andean valley agriculture [@Murra1972; @Stanish2003; @PlattBouysseHarris2006].
Because severe frosts, hailstorms and El Niño droughts periodically curtailed Altiplano potato and quinoa harvests above 3.800 m, highland polities from Tiwanaku through the Aymara *señoríos* and Inca *Qullasuyu* dispatched permanent colony lineages (*mitmaqkuna*) into the Yungas, Larecaja, Cochabamba, Mizque, Chuquisaca and coastal Moquegua-Azapa valleys [@Janusek2008; @GyarmatiVarga1999].
Llama pack-trains numbering hundreds of animals traversed established highland passes linking the Lake Titicaca basin, Oruro and the Salar de Uyuni to Cochabamba maize granaries, eastern coca terraces and Pacific marine salt flats [@Nielsen2002; @BauerStanish2001].

Metallurgical production constituted a second structural pillar of highland nucleation.
Rich polymetallic ore veins across the Eastern Cordillera tin-silver belt — centred on Porco, Potosí, Oruro-Paria, San Cristóbal de Lípez and the copper-tin deposits of Corocoro and Carabuco — supported specialised wind-draft smelting furnaces (*wayras*) centuries before Spanish arrival [@VanBuren2003; @Capriles2023Review].
Geoarchaeological lead-isotope archives recovered from Lake Titicaca, Laguna Lobato near Potosí and the Quelccaya ice cap document sustained pre-Hispanic silver and tin-bronze smelting beginning during the Late Formative and intensifying sharply under Tiwanaku (600AD to 1000AD) and Inca *Qullasuyu* administration (1450AD to 1532AD) [@AbbottWolfe2003; @VanBuren2003].
This combination of raised-field lacustrine surpluses, terraced valley maize production, camelid pastoralism and metallurgical craft specialisation explains why the Bolivian Highlands maintained urban centres exceeding 10k to 35k residents for more than a millennium prior to European contact.

## Comparative Historiography of Highland Bolivian Demography

Earlier global compilations underestimated pre-Columbian Upper Peru because they aggregated the Altiplano either into sparse lowland projections or into undifferentiated Peruvian totals [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008].
Regional reconstructions anchored to Lake Titicaca pedestrian survey transects [@AlbarracinJordan1992; @Bandy2001; @BauerStanish2001], raised-field caloric modelling [@Kolata1993], Cochabamba Inca state granary inventories [@GyarmatiVarga1999] and early sixteenth-century Charcas tributary extrapolations [@PlattBouysseHarris2006] consistently place the Late Horizon population of Highland Bolivia between 1,1M and 1,6M inhabitants.
PRETA's central estimate of 1,41M in 1500AD — declining to 1,25M by 1535AD after the first Eurasian pandemic wave and Inca civil war — sits squarely within this scholarly consensus.
Crucially, pairing this highland curve with the 345k to 380k Casarabe-Moxos lowland baseline restores the historically attested demographic balance of Bolivia across both archaeological and documentary horizons:
1. Lake Titicaca and Tiwanaku anchor the continent's earliest monumental Altiplano urbanism, reaching 320k residents across 28,8k km² by 1500AD (1.111,2 persons per 100 km²).
2. The temperate inter-Andean maize basins of Cochabamba, Chuquiabo-La Paz and Charcas sustain dense agrarian communities exceeding 350 to 460 persons per 100 km².
3. The arid pastoral Altiplano of Oruro, Carangas and Lípez supports lower but resilient agro-pastoral densities linked by long-distance caravan routes [@Nielsen2002; @McAndrews2005].
4. Across the eastern cordillera escarpment, Llanos de Moxos emerges clearly as Bolivia's premier lowland hearth without artificially eclipsing Tiwanaku, La Paz, Cochabamba or Potosí.

## Sub-Regional Multi-Horizon Trajectory Matrix

Table \ref{tab:matrix} disaggregates the highland demographic curve across all six HydroBASINS Level 6 divisions at eleven diagnostic benchmark horizons from 10000BC through 1535AD, illustrating the early lacustrine leadership of Titicaca-Tiwanaku, the Middle Horizon Tiwanaku apogee, the twelfth-century demographic shift toward fortified Aymara *señorío* valleys and the Late Horizon expansion of Cochabamba and La Paz under Inca state granary colonisation.

```{r tbl-matrix, results='asis'}
mat_yrs <- c("-10000", "-5000", "-2000", "-1000", "0", "400", "800", "1000", "1200", "1500", "1535")
mat_hdr <- c("10000BC", "5000BC", "2000BC", "1000BC", "0AD", "400AD", "800AD", "1000AD", "1200AD", "1500AD", "1535AD")
mat_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(mat_yrs, function (yk) viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(r$population[[yk]])), character(1))
  lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_lbls[[rk]])) reg_lbls[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name)
  c(lbl, vals)
})
tot_vals <- vapply(mat_yrs, function (yk) {
  viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]]))
}, character(1))
mat_df <- as.data.frame(rbind(do.call(rbind, mat_rows), c("Bolivian Highlands Total", tot_vals)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
viscount_table(
  mat_df,
  "Multi-horizon demographic trajectories across the six Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands hydrological divisions (10000BC to 1535AD).",
  c("Hydrological Division", mat_hdr),
  list(label = "tab:matrix", font_size = "scriptsize", scale_to_fit = TRUE)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Archaeological Coverage and Gazetteer Density

To verify that no highland sub-region suffers from registry starvation relative to neighbouring Peru, Table \ref{tab:coverage} reports catalogued settlement counts, territorial share, site density per 10.000 km² and summed site peaks across each hydrological division.
All six basins achieve dense empirical coverage, with Lake Titicaca-Tiwanaku (22,9 catalogued sites per 10.000 km²) and Chuquiabo-La Paz-Yungas (11,3 sites per 10.000 km²) matching the survey density of adjacent Peruvian Altiplano catchments.

```{r tbl-coverage, results='asis'}
cov_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  sub_s <- Filter(function (s) identical(s$region_id, rk) || identical(s$region, rk), set_list)
  sub_pks <- if (length(sub_s) > 0) vapply(sub_s, function (s) max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population))), numeric(1)) else 0
  a_km2 <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  data.frame(
    Division = if (!is.null(reg_lbls[[rk]])) reg_lbls[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(a_km2, 0L),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_s)),
    SiteDens = viscount_fmt_number(length(sub_s) / a_km2 * 10000, 1L),
    PeakSum = viscount_fmt_pop(sum(sub_pks)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_cov <- do.call(rbind, cov_rows)
df_cov <- rbind(df_cov, data.frame(
  Division = "Total Bolivian Highlands",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L),
  Sites = as.character(length(set_list)),
  SiteDens = viscount_fmt_number(length(set_list) / tot_area * 10000, 1L),
  PeakSum = viscount_fmt_pop(sum(pks)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))
viscount_table(
  df_cov,
  "Sub-regional archaeological gazetteer coverage, catalogued site density per 10.000 km² and summed site peaks across the Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands.",
  c("Hydrological Division", "Area (km²)", "Sites", "Sites / 10k km²", "Peak Sum"),
  list(label = "tab:coverage", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Uncertainty Envelopes and Sensitivity Bounds

Empirical uncertainty intervals in Table \ref{tab:benchmarks} widen symmetrically backward in time to reflect archaeological visibility constraints.
Across the early and middle Holocene (10000BC to 2000BC), where mobile foraging bands left dispersed lithic scatters and cave occupations, headline totals carry a plus-or-minus 35% uncertainty envelope (for example, 125,5k to 260,7k around the 193,1k estimate for 2000BC).
From the Formative consolidation through the Late Intermediate Period (1000BC to 1400AD), pedestrian survey site-area densities and Bayesian radiocarbon chronologies narrow the uncertainty envelope to plus-or-minus 25% (900k to 1,50M around the 1,20M Tiwanaku peak in 800AD).
On the eve of Spanish conquest (1500AD to 1535AD), cross-validation against early colonial *repartimiento* tributary rolls and Viceroy Toledo's 1572AD to 1575AD *Visita General* constrains regional uncertainty to plus-or-minus 18% (1,16M to 1,66M in 1500AD; 1,03M to 1,48M in 1535AD).

## Continuity into Colonial Charcas (1535AD)

To preserve annual demographic continuity across Bolivia from 10000BC to 2026AD without artificial boundary cliffs, the terminal benchmark of this chapter (1,25M inhabitants in 1535AD across the six highland hydrological divisions) matches the opening 1535AD baseline of PRETA's Colonial Bolivian Highlands (Real Audiencia de Charcas) chapter identically.
At the sub-regional scale, Lake Titicaca and Chuquiabo-La Paz flow directly into the Intendencia de La Paz (430k in 1535AD).
Central Altiplano Wankarani-Paria-Carangas flows into Oruro (145k), and Cochabamba-Mizque flows into the Intendencia de Cochabamba (255k).
Finally, the Charcas-Potosí-Chuquisaca-Tarija cordillera divisions flow directly into Chuquisaca (155k), Potosí (210k) and Tarija (55k).
Together with the lowland Bolivian savannas tracked in the Western Amazon Basin and Colonial Spanish Amazon chapters, this architecture guarantees uninterrupted spatial and demographic coherence across the entirety of Bolivia.
All sub-regional masks sum strictly without overlap or gap to the full pre-Columbian highland footprint.
The accompanying settlement gazetteer provides full coordinate provenance for all 316 pre-Hispanic localities.
Every demographic benchmark reconciles directly against the regional substrata raster stack.
Both the archaeological site density layer and the calibrated 5-arcminute population rasters confirm that Highland Bolivia maintained three- to ten-fold higher demographic intensity than the eastern tropical lowlands throughout the late Holocene.
